name: Welfare State
description: There is a country with $$$n$$$ citizens. The $$$i$$$-th of them initially has $$$a_{i}$$$ money. The government strictly controls the wealth of its citizens. Whenever a citizen makes a purchase or earns some money, they must send a receipt to the social services mentioning the amount of money they currently have. Sometimes the government makes payouts to the poor: all citizens who have strictly less money than $$$x$$$ are paid accordingly so that after the payout they have exactly $$$x$$$ money. In this case the citizens don't send a receipt. You know the initial wealth of every citizen and the log of all events: receipts and payouts. Restore the amount of money each citizen has after all events.
input_specification: The first line contains a single integer $$$n$$$ ($$$1 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^{5}$$$) — the numer of citizens. The next line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$a_1$$$, $$$a_2$$$, ..., $$$a_n$$$ ($$$0 \le a_{i} \le 10^{9}$$$) — the initial balances of citizens. The next line contains a single integer $$$q$$$ ($$$1 \le q \le 2 \cdot 10^{5}$$$) — the number of events. Each of the next $$$q$$$ lines contains a single event. The events are given in chronological order. Each event is described as either 1 p x ($$$1 \le p \le n$$$, $$$0 \le x \le 10^{9}$$$), or 2 x ($$$0 \le x \le 10^{9}$$$). In the first case we have a receipt that the balance of the $$$p$$$-th person becomes equal to $$$x$$$. In the second case we have a payoff with parameter $$$x$$$.
output_specification: Print $$$n$$$ integers — the balances of all citizens after all events.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1198B — Welfare State [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
